section.title: The Oracle against Moab
section.sectionRationale: The third and longest of the smaller oracles against the nations turns to Moab, Israel's kin through Lot and a long-time rival across the Jordan. Town after Moabite town is named and mourned, Moab's pride and trust in Chemosh and in her own wealth are exposed, and even the LORD Himself is pictured weeping over her, before the oracle ends with an unexpected promise of restoration in the latter days.
section.thesis: Moab is broken for trusting her own works, wealth, and god Chemosh instead of the LORD; yet the same LORD who shatters her like an unwanted jar weeps for her fall and promises to restore her in the latter days.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: woe to Moab's proud cities; trust in wealth and Chemosh ends in exile; the scepter shattered, mourning across every town; ridicule for the proud, drunk on judgment; the LORD Himself weeps for Moab; universal mourning, shattered like an unwanted jar; and the eagle, the pit, and the snare, yet mercy in the latter days.

verses.text: Concerning Moab, this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Woe to Nebo, for it will be devastated. Kiriathaim will be captured and disgraced; the fortress will be shattered and dismantled.
There is no longer praise for Moab; in Heshbon they devise evil against her: ‘Come, let us cut her off from nationhood.’ You too, O people of Madmen, will be silenced; the sword will pursue you.
A voice cries out from Horonaim: ‘Devastation and great destruction!’
Moab will be shattered; her little ones will cry out.
For on the ascent to Luhith they weep bitterly as they go, and on the descent to Horonaim cries of distress resound over the destruction:
‘Flee! Run for your lives! Become like a juniper in the desert.’

units.label: Trust in wealth and Chemosh ends in exile
units.note: settled on the dregs, soon poured out

verses.text: Because you trust in your works and treasures, you too will be captured, and {{chemosh|Chemosh}} will go into exile with his priests and officials.
The destroyer will move against every city, and not one town will escape. The valley will also be ruined, and the high plain will be destroyed, as the LORD has said.
Put salt on Moab, for she will be laid waste; her cities will become desolate, with no one to dwell in them.
Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed.
Moab has been at ease from youth, settled like wine on its dregs; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel or gone into exile. So his flavor has remained the same, and his aroma is unchanged.
Therefore behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will send to him wanderers, who will pour him out. They will empty his vessels and shatter his jars.
Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed when they trusted in Bethel.

units.label: The scepter shattered, mourning across every town
units.note: boasting brought low, a roll call of ruins

verses.text: How can you say, ‘We are warriors, mighty men ready for battle’?
Moab has been destroyed and its towns have been invaded; the best of its young men have gone down in the slaughter, declares the King, whose name is the LORD of Hosts.
Moab’s calamity is at hand, and his affliction is rushing swiftly.
Mourn for him, all you who surround him, everyone who knows his name; tell how the mighty scepter is shattered, the glorious staff!
Come down from your glory; sit on parched ground, O daughter dwelling in Dibon, for the destroyer of Moab has come against you; he has destroyed your fortresses.
Stand by the road and watch, O dweller of Aroer! Ask the man fleeing or the woman escaping, ‘What has happened?’
Moab is put to shame, for it has been shattered. Wail and cry out! Declare by the Arnon that Moab is destroyed.
Judgment has come upon the high plain: upon Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath,
upon Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim,
upon Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon,
upon Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the towns of Moab, those far and near.
The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm is broken,” declares the LORD.

units.label: Ridicule for the proud, drunk on judgment

verses.text: “Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD; so Moab will wallow in his own vomit, and he will also become a laughingstock.
Was not Israel your object of ridicule? Was he ever found among thieves? For whenever you speak of him you shake your head.
Abandon the towns and settle among the rocks, O dwellers of Moab! Be like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave.

units.label: The LORD Himself weeps for Moab

verses.text: We have heard of Moab’s {{gaon|pomposity}}, his exceeding pride and conceit, his proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart.
I know his insolence,” declares the LORD, “but it is futile. His boasting is as empty as his deeds.
Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab; I will moan for the men of Kir-heres.

I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah, more than I weep for Jazer. Your tendrils have extended to the sea; they reach even to Jazer. The destroyer has descended on your summer fruit and grape harvest.
Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard and from the fields of Moab. I have stopped the flow of wine from the presses; no one treads them with shouts of joy; their shouts are not for joy.
There is a cry from Heshbon to Elealeh; they raise their voices to Jahaz, from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah; for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up.
In Moab, declares the LORD, I will bring an end to those who make offerings on the high places and burn incense to their gods.
Therefore My heart laments like a flute for Moab; it laments like a flute for the men of Kir-heres, because the wealth they acquired has perished.

units.label: Universal mourning, shattered like an unwanted jar

verses.text: For every head is shaved and every beard is clipped; on every hand is a gash, and around every waist is sackcloth.
On all the rooftops of Moab and in the public squares, everyone is mourning; for I have shattered Moab like an unwanted jar,” declares the LORD.
“How shattered it is! How they wail! How Moab has turned his back in shame! Moab has become an object of ridicule and horror to all those around him.”

units.label: The eagle, the pit, and the snare, yet mercy in the latter days

verses.text: For this is what the LORD says: “Behold, an eagle swoops down and spreads his wings against Moab.
Kirioth has been taken, and the strongholds seized. In that day the heart of Moab’s warriors will be like the heart of a woman in labor.
Moab will be destroyed as a nation because he vaunted himself against the LORD.
Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab,” declares the LORD.
“Whoever flees the panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare. For I will bring upon Moab the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD.
“Those who flee will stand helpless in Heshbon’s shadow, because fire has gone forth from Heshbon and a flame from within Sihon. It devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult.
Woe to you, O Moab! The people of Chemosh have perished; for your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.
Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,” declares the LORD. Here ends the judgment on Moab.

chemosh.gloss: Chemosh, the national god of Moab, to whom Moabite kings offered sacrifice, even child sacrifice in extremity, 2 Kings 3:27. That Chemosh goes into exile with his own priests, verse 7, shows he cannot save the people who trusted him.

gaon.gloss: Pride, pomposity, or exaltation, here describing Moab's proud arrogance and haughtiness of heart, verse 29. The same root can describe legitimate majesty, but turned toward self, it becomes the very thing the LORD opposes and brings down.

basic.context: This is the longest of the shorter oracles against the nations, aimed at Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot, Israel's kin and frequent rival. Town after Moabite town, Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Dibon, Kerioth, and more, is named and mourned in turn. Moab's sin is trust in her own works, wealth, and long ease, and in Chemosh her god, none of which can save her when the destroyer comes; yet astonishingly, the LORD Himself is pictured weeping over Moab's fall, and the oracle ends with a promise of restoration.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes an actual historical judgment on Moab, largely fulfilled through Babylonian campaigns in the early sixth century BC that ended Moab's existence as a distinct kingdom. It is not a coded message about any nation today. The lasting truth is that ease and self-sufficiency, settling like wine undisturbed on its dregs, make a people brittle rather than strong, and that no idol can rescue those who trust it.
basic.originalLanguages: Chemosh, Moab's national god, is named three times, always to show his helplessness: he goes into exile with his own priests, verse 7, and his people perish with him, verse 46. Moab's core sin is named with the word ga'own, pride or pomposity, verse 29, the same haughtiness of heart that runs through every oracle against the nations in this section.
basic.typology: Moab shattered like an unwanted jar, verse 38, pictures the fate of every vessel of wrath prepared for destruction, Romans 9:22, in contrast to vessels of mercy prepared beforehand for glory. The LORD's own weeping over Moab, verses 31 to 36, anticipates Christ weeping over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41, the same divine grief poured out even upon those under righteous judgment.
basic.christ: Remarkably, the LORD does not merely announce Moab's judgment; He weeps for it, wailing and moaning like a flute in lament, verses 31 to 36. That grief over necessary judgment finds its clearest echo in Christ, who wept over Jerusalem even while pronouncing the very judgment that was coming upon her, Luke 19:41 to 44. And where Moab's pride and trust in Chemosh brought her down, Christ is the one truly exalted King who humbled Himself and was therefore lifted up, Philippians 2:8-9, the opposite pattern to Moab's proud fall.
basic.god: God opposes pride absolutely: Moab's ga'own, her proud arrogance, is named as the very root of her downfall, verse 29. Yet God's justice is never cold; He grieves even as He judges, and He does not close the book on Moab forever, promising restoration in the latter days, verse 47, the same shape of mercy folded into judgment found throughout these oracles.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 21:29 and Isaiah 15 to 16 give earlier oracles against Moab. 2 Kings 3:27 records Moab's king offering his own son to Chemosh in desperation. Luke 19:41-44 shows Christ weeping over Jerusalem's coming judgment. Romans 9:22 speaks of vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, echoing the image of Moab shattered like a jar.
basic.oneStory: Moab's proud self-sufficiency and trust in Chemosh could not save her from the LORD's justice, yet the same LORD who judged her wept over her fall and promised restoration in the latter days. That pattern, judgment held together with grief and hope, comes to its fullest expression in Christ, who wept over Jerusalem even as He went to bear judgment Himself, so that mercy might reach every proud nation humbled before God.

context.literary:
At forty seven verses, Jeremiah 48 is the longest chapter given to a single nation in the oracles against the nations apart from Babylon, and it is built as a funeral procession through a map. Verses 1 to 6 begin at Nebo and Kiriathaim and run through Heshbon, Madmen and Horonaim, with a cry going out from each. The catalogue returns in verses 21 to 24, where Holon, Jahzah, Mephaath, Dibon, Nebo, Beth-diblathaim, Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon and Kerioth are listed in clipped runs of three. The lists are not filler. They tell Moab that the whole country, far and near, is already on the sentence.

The chapter's second structure is a family of images for ease and its end. Wine is the main one. Moab is wine settled on its dregs that has never been poured from vessel to vessel, verse 11. The LORD will send wanderers who pour him out and shatter his jars, verse 12. The nation will be made drunk and will wallow in its own vomit, verse 26. The winepresses fall silent, verse 33. And finally Moab is 'an unwanted jar' that the LORD has shattered, verse 38. The same vessel runs from comfort to ruin.

The voice turns at verse 29. Up to verse 28 the LORD announces and the prophet commands the mourners. From verse 29 to 36 the poem presses into a rare place: 'I will wail for Moab,' 'I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah,' 'My heart laments like a flute.' Then verses 37 to 39 return to the public grief of shaved heads and sackcloth, and verses 40 to 46 give a final run of beasts and traps: an eagle, a pit and a snare. Verse 47 closes with a promise and a colophon, 'Here ends the judgment on Moab.' Most of the middle of the poem, verses 29 to 38, runs very close to Isaiah 15 and 16, and Jeremiah has clearly taken up an older oracle and made it his own.
context.historical:
Moab lay on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the gorge of the Arnon in the north and the territory of Edom in the south. The Moabites traced their descent to Moab, the son of Lot's elder daughter, Genesis 19:37, which is why Israel was told not to harass them when they passed, Deuteronomy 2:9. Relations were stormy all the same. Balak hired Balaam against Israel, Numbers 22 to 24, which is the reason Deuteronomy 23:3-4 bars Moabites from the assembly, and Nehemiah 13:1-2 recalls it. Yet Ruth the Moabitess became the great-grandmother of David, Ruth 4:17, and Matthew 1:5 names her in the line of the Messiah.

Chemosh is Moab's national god. Judges 11:24 has Jephthah speak of 'your god Chemosh' as Ammon's, which is a puzzle noted by students of Judges, and 1 Kings 11:7 records Solomon building a high place for 'Chemosh the abomination of Moab.' A Moabite stone of King Mesha, found in the nineteenth century and not part of Scripture, names Chemosh as the god who gave Mesha victory and records places such as Dibon and Nebo that appear in Jeremiah's lists. The Bible tells of the same king at 2 Kings 3:4-27, where in a moment of desperation he offers his own son on the city wall.

The oracle belongs to the years when Judah's neighbours debated whether to join a revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah 27:3 has envoys of Moab, Edom, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon in Jerusalem during Zedekiah's reign, and 2 Kings 24:2 records Moabite raiders sent against Jehoiakim 'according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servants the prophets.' Ezekiel 25:8-11 charges Moab with saying that the house of Judah is like all the other nations. The sixth century saw Moab swallowed by Babylon and then by the desert tribes of the east. The text does not date the fall precisely, and it is best to say the judgment came with the Babylonian domination of the region, not in a single campaign.
context.canonical:
Jeremiah 48 is an extended meditation on a tradition older than itself. Numbers 21:28-29 already sang of a fire from Heshbon that consumed Ar of Moab and of 'the people of Chemosh' made refugees. Jeremiah 48:45-46 turns that old song around: now fire comes out of Heshbon against Moab, and the people of Chemosh perish. Numbers 24:17 had promised a star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel who 'will crush the skulls of Moab,' and Jeremiah 48:45 speaks of 'the skulls of the sons of tumult,' keeping the old image alive. The verse about proud Moab, 'we have heard of Moab's pomposity,' appears almost word for word in Isaiah 16:6, and the laments over the vines of Sibmah and the silenced winepresses in verses 32 and 33 recall Isaiah 16:8-10. Isaiah 25:10-11 sets Moab's pride beside the LORD's mountain and promises it will be brought low.

The other prophets round out the picture. Amos 2:1-3 condemns Moab for burning the bones of Edom's king to lime. Zephaniah 2:8-11 charges Moab and Ammon with mocking His people and promises that 'the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him.' Ezekiel 25:8-11 names Moab's contempt for Judah. The final word about Moab's mercy appears in Ruth, in the line of David, and in Matthew 1:5.

The New Testament does not quote Jeremiah 48 by name, but it takes up its themes. James 4:6 says 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,' and Luke 12:19-20 tells the story of a man who tells himself to eat, drink and be merry, a portrait of Moab settled on his dregs. Luke 19:41 shows Jesus weeping over Jerusalem as the LORD wept over Moab. And Philippians 2:9-11 speaks of a day when every knee will bow, which is the full width of what verse 47 hints at.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah has been telling Judah for decades that Babylon is the LORD's servant and that rebellion against Babylon is rebellion against God, Jeremiah 27:6-7. When Moab's envoys sit in Jerusalem planning an uprising, Jeremiah 27:3, this chapter tells Judah what will happen to a nation that trusts its works and treasures, verse 7. Moab is a mirror. Judah's own sins are different in detail, but the pattern is the same: long ease, a settled sense of safety, a god who cannot save.

The chapter also teaches Judah how to hold judgment without gloating. The oracle does not stand on a mountain and cheer. It sends mourners through the towns and has the LORD Himself speak in the first person about wailing. First hearers who might have been tempted to take satisfaction in the fall of an old enemy are told that the God who ordains the fall grieves over it, and that He has a future for Moab, verse 47. The point is meant to shape how Judah regards the nations: not as targets of hatred, but as peoples under the same Judge whose mercy reaches further than their histories.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records the sentence on one nation at one time. It does not command believers to see any current people as Moab, and it does not permit anyone to wish ruin on a group. The one imperative that could be misread is verse 10, 'Cursed is the one who is remiss in doing the work of the LORD, and cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed.' That line addresses the human instruments the LORD is sending to carry out this specific judgment. It does not enlist later readers in violence, and nothing in the New Testament applies it that way.

What carries forward is the warning about comfort. 'Moab has been at ease from youth' is a description of a spiritual condition that believers recognise: unshaken, unrefined, trusting works and treasures. The right response is the one the chapter itself models, to weep with the LORD where He weeps, and to take the warning home. As 1 Corinthians 10:12 says, the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 31 to 36, 'I will wail for Moab'?

views.label: The LORD Himself
views.case: The speech is framed with 'I know his insolence,' declares the LORD, verse 30, and the 'My heart laments' of verse 36 leaves no other speaker in view. Hosea 11:8 and Genesis 6:6 show the LORD's heart moved by those He judges. On this reading the weeping is the LORD's own and is a genuine statement of divine grief.

views.label: The prophet speaking for the LORD
views.case: Isaiah 15:5 and 16:9-11 use the same words in the prophet's own voice, 'My heart cries out over Moab,' 'I weep.' Some propose that Jeremiah is quoting Isaiah's lament as the prophet's own response, so that the grief is a shared one, the prophet's heart in tune with the LORD's.

views.label: A poetic figure of speech for divine regret
views.case: Others treat the weeping as human language for God's seriousness about sin and judgment, an anthropopathism, without implying that God experiences sorrow as we do.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the text has joined two truths without softening either: the sentence stands, and the one who passes it grieves. Verse 36 sets the lament in the first person of the LORD and so gives the strongest reading, but the point does not depend on settling the grammar. The prophet and the LORD are not speaking against each other.

debates.question: What does the promise of verse 47, 'in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity,' mean?

views.label: A historical return of Moabite exiles
views.case: The phrase can be read as a promise that exiles of Moab would return to their land, as Judah's were. The BSB footnote renders the phrase 'restore the fortunes of Moab,' which allows a broader sense of renewal.

views.label: Fulfilled in the gospel reaching the nations
views.case: Because the prophets use 'latter days' for the age of the Messiah, many Christian readers take the promise as a sign that Moab's people are included in the gospel, as Ruth the Moabitess was included in the line of David, Ruth 4:17, Matthew 1:5. Acts 2:9-11 and Ephesians 2:11-13 are used to show the same widening.

views.label: A promise held for the new creation
views.case: A third view holds that the final restoration awaits the new heavens and new earth, where the nations are healed, Revelation 21:24 and 22:2, and that the promise belongs there.

debates.bearing: The text itself does not say how, only that the LORD's last word over Moab is restoration. The three readings do not exclude each other. What is solid is the shape: the God who shatters the jar is the God who promises, and the Bible's own pattern of Gentile inclusion makes that promise credible.

study.originalLanguages:
The basic level has named Chemosh and the word for pride. Five other features of the Hebrew show how the poem is made.

First, the poem is full of sounds. The BSB footnotes mark two of them. At verse 2 the name Heshbon sounds like the Hebrew for 'plot,' and the town is said to plot evil, and Madmen sounds like the Hebrew for 'silenced,' and the town is told it will be silenced. Moab's towns are punished in the sound of their own names, which is the prophets' way of saying that judgment fits. Verse 6 has a similar ambiguity. The BSB reads 'become like a juniper in the desert,' with a footnote that the word may be a wild donkey or a place name, Aroer. The idea is the same either way: flee like something that survives only by running.

Second, verse 9 reads in the BSB 'Put salt on Moab,' and the footnote adds 'Or Give wings to Moab, for she would fly away.' The Hebrew word that can mean either salt or a wing is uncertain, and translators divide. Salt would point to the sowing of a ruined land with salt, as in the curse on a city, and the wings read would make Moab flee. Both meanings fit the surrounding ruin, and readers should not rest anything weighty on either.

Third, verse 11 describes Moab as wine 'settled on its dregs.' The idiom belongs to the winemaker's craft. Wine left on its lees without being poured from vessel to vessel keeps its strength and its flavour, which sounds like a compliment until the image is turned. In Zephaniah 1:12 the same picture describes men 'settled in complacency' who think the LORD will do nothing, good or bad. Moab's ease is a spiritual fault, and the wanderers sent in verse 12 are the pouring that was never done.

Fourth, the ruin is always shattered, a verb of breakage repeated through the chapter. The jar is 'unwanted,' verse 38, which means a vessel nobody values enough to keep. The same language of a broken vessel runs through Jeremiah, notably the potter's flask smashed in chapter 19. Moab is treated like the flask.

Fifth, verse 10 includes the harsh line, 'cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed.' The word for 'remiss' means slack or deceitful in doing a job. The verse is addressed to the human agents who will do the LORD's work, and it warns them not to treat a commission lightly. It is the same reasoning as the appointed sword in chapter 47.

Finally, the closing verse uses the ordinary idiom for restoring captivity. The BSB footnote renders it 'restore the fortunes of Moab,' and the phrase can carry either a return from exile or a wider reversal. Jeremiah uses the same idiom for Judah in Jeremiah 30:3 and 32:44, which sets Moab's hope in the same grammar as Israel's.

typology.type: Moab settled on his dregs, Jeremiah 48:11
typology.fulfillment: Ease that has never been tested looks like strength until it is poured out. Jesus tells of a rich man who says to himself 'Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry,' and God says 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you,' Luke 12:19-20, and the Lord's own words to the church in Laodicea about being rich and in need of nothing run along the same lines, Revelation 3:17. The correspondence is the self-sufficiency that cannot survive God's question. The type falls short because Moab's story is about a nation's fate, while Luke 12 addresses each person, and the pattern ends in Christ's offer of true riches, not in ruin alone.

typology.type: The vessel shattered and the vessel of mercy, Jeremiah 48:38
typology.fulfillment: The jar nobody wants is broken by the LORD. Paul takes up the image of vessels at Romans 9:22-23, where there are vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy, and 2 Corinthians 4:7 says believers hold treasure in jars of clay. In Christ the jar is not thrown away but renewed: the one who was broken for His people makes them vessels for honour. The type falls short because Jeremiah's jar is smashed, and Paul's vessels of mercy are kept. And verse 47 promises that even Moab's vessel will be restored.

typology.type: The star who crushes the skulls of Moab, Numbers 24:17 and Jeremiah 48:45
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's fire from Heshbon recalls the words of Balaam's fourth oracle, a star out of Jacob who crushes the skulls of Moab. The magi who come following a star to the born King of the Jews, Matthew 2:2, hear the same sky language, and Revelation 22:16 has Jesus call Himself 'the bright Morning Star.' The correspondence is the Messiah as conqueror of the pride of Moab. The escalation is that He conquers by being lifted up, John 12:32, and the Moabite Ruth stands in His own genealogy, Matthew 1:5.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the grief of verses 31 to 36. A prophet or a God who only pronounced judgment would not say 'I will wail for Moab.' Here the LORD cries out over the destruction of the vines of Sibmah and the silencing of the winepresses, and 'My heart laments like a flute.' When Jesus comes near Jerusalem He weeps, Luke 19:41, and speaks the sentence that is coming at the same moment, Luke 19:43-44. At Lazarus's tomb 'Jesus wept,' John 11:35. The correspondence is not accidental. It shows that the sentence and the sorrow belong to the same heart, and the Son reveals that heart in a human face.

It leads to Christ by the contrast of pride and humility. Moab is condemned for magnifying himself against the LORD, verse 26, and for 'pomposity... exceeding pride and conceit,' verse 29. The Servant 'humbled Himself' and was 'exalted to the highest place,' Philippians 2:8-9, so that every knee bows to Him, Philippians 2:10, the homage Moab refused to the LORD. Moab is told to 'come down from your glory,' verse 18, and the Son came down to the lowest place. Proud Moab is humbled by the LORD, and Christ is exalted by the Father because He humbled Himself.

It leads to Christ by the star. Balaam saw from a distance a star from Jacob who would crush the skulls of Moab, Numbers 24:17. Jeremiah's use of that tradition in verse 45 shows he read Moab's fate as part of the long conflict the King of Israel would settle. The magi are guided by a star in the east to the born King of the Jews, Matthew 2:2, and Revelation 22:16 has Jesus call Himself 'the bright Morning Star.' The ancient oracle and the gospel meet on the same figure.

And it leads to Christ by the promise at the end. The last verse before the colophon says that in the latter days the LORD will restore Moab from captivity. The line of the Messiah passes through a Moabite woman. Ruth says 'your God will be my God,' Ruth 1:16, and she is the great-grandmother of David, Ruth 4:17, and appears in Matthew's genealogy, Matthew 1:5. In Christ 'the dividing wall of hostility' is broken down, Ephesians 2:14, so that those once far off are brought near. The Deuteronomy rule that barred a Moabite from the assembly has been answered in Jesus.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Jeremiah 48 does not mention the Messiah, and the Moabites are not hidden pictures of Christ's enemies. The links above rest on the way the New Testament itself treats pride, weeping, the star and the inclusion of the nations. What the chapter supplies is a God whose grief and justice are one voice, and a promise that the Gospel finally makes credible.
study.god:
The chapter's picture of God begins with His opposition to pride. Moab's fault, verses 26 and 29, is that he has magnified himself against the LORD, and Proverbs 16:18 and James 4:6 treat the same fault as the root of ruin. God does not need an elaborate accusation. The pattern is simple: security built on works and treasures, verse 7, and on a god who cannot save, verse 13, falls when the real Judge acts. Isaiah 2:12 calls this the day of the LORD against everything proud and lofty.

Second, the LORD is sovereign over gods as well as nations. Chemosh 'will go into exile with his priests and officials,' verse 7, and 'the people of Chemosh have perished,' verse 46. Idols in the ancient world were carried in procession, and to carry a god away was to say he had been defeated. Isaiah 46:1-2 makes a similar mockery of Bel and Nebo, who cower and are carried into captivity. The sentence on Chemosh is a lesson in monotheism, and Habakkuk 2:19 says of such gods that there is 'no breath in them at all.'

Third, God is just and measured. The cities are named in order, the sin is named, and the sentence fits it, wine to dregs and dregs to the pouring, ease to the wanderers who unsettle it, verses 11 and 12. He deals with Moab on the principle that He has used with every nation: what a people does to others will be returned. Moab had laughed at Israel's trouble, verse 27, and Amos 2:1-3 says Moab burned the bones of Edom's king.

Fourth, and most surprising, God grieves. 'I will wail for Moab... I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah,' verses 31 and 32. Genesis 6:6 says He was grieved in His heart, and Hosea 11:8 says His compassion is stirred. The wording of Isaiah 15 and 16 is taken up and put in His mouth, so the tradition of Israel was never that the LORD enjoys judgment. Divine impassibility, the idea that God is not at the mercy of emotions, need not be denied to read this. The text says His justice and His compassion are the same person speaking, and neither is a performance.

Fifth, God keeps a future for those He judges. Verse 47 ends with a promise of restoration, and that is how the book of Jeremiah handles other nations too. The oracle ends with a sentence that this is the end of the judgment on Moab, and the tone of the end is hope.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to fear the LORD, to refuse every settled comfort that makes us forget Him, and to weep with Him over those who are broken. It protects believers from two errors: the cold watching of judgment, and the soft denial that judgment is real.

crossReferences.note: Almost word for word the same charge appears here, 'we have heard of Moab's pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit.' Jeremiah 48:29 shows that he is taking over an older oracle and applying it to the generation facing Babylon. The shared words give the charge the weight of tradition.

The prophet weeps for the vines of Sibmah, the silenced winepresses and the laments like a harp. Jeremiah 48:32-36 uses the same laments, which shows that the grief for Moab was part of Israel's prophetic inheritance, not Jeremiah's invention.

An old song recalls a fire from Heshbon that consumed Ar of Moab and calls Moab the 'people of Chemosh.' Jeremiah 48:45-46 echoes both lines and reverses them, as the fire now comes out of Heshbon against Moab.

Balaam sees a star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel who will 'crush the skulls of Moab.' Jeremiah 48:45 speaks of the skulls of Moab's sons, showing the sentence is part of a long-promised outworking, and Christian readers hear in the star the King who is born in Matthew 2:2.

The LORD searches Jerusalem with lamps and punishes 'the men settled in complacency.' The same picture of a people settled on their dregs is used for Judah, and it shows that Moab's fault is not unique to Moab. The mirror is held up to Jerusalem.

The king of Moab, desperate in battle, offers his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall. It gives the strongest scene in the Old Testament of what trust in Chemosh looks like at the end, and it explains why Jeremiah says Chemosh cannot save.

Amos charges Moab with burning to lime the bones of Edom's king and promises fire on the citadels of Kerioth, which Jeremiah 48:24 also names. The two prophets agree that Moab's own violence is part of the charge.

A Moabite woman says to Naomi, 'your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.' Against the oracle's sentence, it shows how Moab can be received into the people of God, and it prepares the line to David and to Christ in Ruth 4:17 and Matthew 1:5.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem as He announces the coming judgment. The pairing of grief and verdict in Jeremiah 48:31-36 finds its fullest echo in the Son, who shows the same heart as the LORD who wept for Moab.

The proud are brought low in Jeremiah 48, and in Philippians the humbled Christ is exalted so that every knee bows. Verse 47's hope that even Moab is restored is the same horizon, where the nations confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the Bible shows human pride as the root of ruin. The fall began with a desire to be like God, Genesis 3:5, and Moab is one of the Bible's pictures of the same instinct carried through a whole people. Moab comes into the story at Genesis 19:37, among the broken fruits of a family that left Abraham's side and a sin in a cave, and the nation that grows from it becomes a neighbour that Israel must pass, Deuteronomy 2:9, a tempter that hires Balaam, Numbers 22 to 24, and a rival whose god is set beside the LORD's in Solomon's own hill-shrines, 1 Kings 11:7.

The oracle answers all that. The LORD who raised up Babylon as His instrument, Jeremiah 27:6, brings the long ease of Moab to an end and shows Chemosh to be a god that must be carried into exile. This is the same pattern the Bible has run since Egypt, where the LORD executed judgment on the gods of Egypt, and since Babel, where a human tower was brought down. The pride of man and the powerlessness of idols are the fixed points of the story.

But the oracle also sets up the other side of the story. A God who wails for Moab and promises to restore her is a God who intends to have the nations. The line leads through Ruth, a Moabite woman who clings to Naomi and says 'your God will be my God,' Ruth 1:16. She becomes the great-grandmother of David, Ruth 4:17, and appears in the genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5. The prophets look further. Zephaniah 2:11 sees the nations of every shore bowing to the LORD, each in its own place. The old wall that kept Moabites out of the assembly, Deuteronomy 23:3, is torn down in Christ, 'the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14.

The story ends in the new creation, where the proud are gone and the nations are healed. The pomp that Moab loved gives way to a city where the kings of the earth bring their glory in, Revelation 21:24, and the tree of life is for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The God who wept over the vines of Sibmah is the God who will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:4. In that city the jar that was broken is made new, and the people of Chemosh, with every other people, may have a place at the table of the Lamb.

quiz.q: According to verse 7, what does Moab trust in that will not save her?

options.text: Her own works and treasures, alongside her god Chemosh.
options.note: Verse 7 names this exact combination of self-reliance and false worship as the reason for Moab's capture.

options.text: Her alliance with Egypt.
options.note: No Egyptian alliance is mentioned in this oracle; the failure named is trust in works, treasure, and Chemosh.

options.text: Her army's superior weapons.
options.note: Moab's warriors are addressed later in the chapter, but the specific trust named in verse 7 is her works, treasures, and Chemosh.

options.text: Her covenant with the LORD.
options.note: Moab was never in covenant with the LORD; her trust was in her own works and in Chemosh.

quiz.q: What image describes Moab's long, untroubled ease in verse 11?

options.text: Wine settled undisturbed on its dregs, never poured from vessel to vessel.
options.note: Verse 11 uses exactly this image to describe Moab's untested comfort.

options.text: A tree planted by flowing streams.
options.note: This is a positive image used elsewhere in Scripture, not the image used here.

options.text: A city built on solid rock.
options.note: Not the image in this passage; Moab's stability is pictured as false ease, not sound foundation.

options.text: A field left fallow for planting.
options.note: Related in spirit to untouched stillness, but the specific image given is wine settled on its dregs.

quiz.q: How does the LORD respond to Moab's coming judgment in verses 31 to 36?

options.text: He weeps and laments for Moab like a mourning flute, even while pronouncing her judgment.
options.note: These verses show the LORD Himself grieving Moab's fall, a striking picture of justice joined with sorrow.

options.text: He rejoices openly over her downfall.
options.note: The opposite is shown; the LORD mourns rather than celebrates Moab's ruin.

options.text: He remains entirely silent about Moab's fate.
options.note: The LORD speaks extensively and personally throughout this chapter.

options.text: He blames Israel for provoking Moab's judgment.
options.note: Not the content of these verses; the LORD's grief here is directed at Moab's own fall, not at Israel's role.

quiz.q: What hope closes the oracle against Moab in verse 47?

options.text: The LORD promises to restore Moab from captivity in the latter days.
options.note: Verse 47 explicitly holds out this hope even after such thorough judgment.

options.text: Moab is promised she will never again face any judgment.
options.note: Overstated; judgment on Moab is very real, but restoration is promised for a future day.

options.text: Moab will conquer all her former enemies.
options.note: No such promise appears; the hope given is restoration, not conquest.

options.text: There is no hope offered for Moab at all.
options.note: Verse 47 explicitly offers hope of restoration in the latter days.

quiz.q: How does the LORD's weeping over Moab anticipate Christ?

options.text: It foreshadows Christ weeping over Jerusalem even as He pronounced her coming judgment.
options.note: Luke 19:41-44 shows Christ grieving over the very judgment He announces, echoing this same pattern.

options.text: It shows that God never actually judges anyone.
options.note: The chapter is full of real, severe judgment on Moab; grief does not cancel justice.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Scripture draws a clear parallel between this divine grief and Christ's tears over Jerusalem.

options.text: It suggests judgment is always a mistake to be regretted.
options.note: The grief shown is sorrow over necessary judgment, not regret that it was wrong to bring it.

questions: Moab had settled like wine undisturbed on its dregs, never tested by hardship. Where has comfort made you complacent rather than dependent on God?
Moab's pride, her ga'own, is named as the root of her fall. Where does pride quietly shape your own decisions or self-image?
Chemosh could not save the people who trusted him, and went into exile with them. What are you trusting that, in the end, cannot actually deliver you?
The LORD wept even as He judged Moab. How does it change your view of God's justice to know that He takes no delight in judgment, even when it is deserved?
Even after such thorough judgment, the LORD promised to restore Moab in the latter days. Where do you need to believe that God's mercy can still reach a situation you have written off as beyond hope?
